text: One of Jost Amman's pupils said the drawings he made in four years would have filled a hay wagon. About 1,500 prints are attributed to him, and many of his original drawings are in the Berlin print room. He was the son of a professor of Classics and Logic in Zürich and moved to Nuremberg in 1560, where he worked first with Virgil Solis. He was one of the last major producers of woodcuts for books, as engravings were gradually taking over that role. Like most woodcut artists, he normally let a specialist cut the block. He died in 1591.

Jean Mariette came from a line of wealthy print publishers, his father Pierre II and his grandfather Pierre I. He studied drawing, painting and engraving with his brother-in-law Jean-Baptiste Corneille, but he stopped painting after Charles Le Brun saw some of his engravings and advised him to focus on that. After his father's death he took over one of the family businesses on the rue Saint-Jacques. Over his career he published almost 900 prints. He was the father of Pierre-Jean Mariette and died in 1742.

William Callow was apprenticed to Copley Fielding, who taught him plein air sketching, and he went on to study under Theodore and Thales Fielding, where he learned to colour prints and make aquatints. In 1829 Thales found him work as an engraver in Paris, alongside his friend Charles Bentley. After he showed a watercolour of Richmond Hill at the Paris Salon of 1831, he was offered a job teaching the family of King Louis Philippe. For several years he gave lessons to the Duc de Nemours and Princess Clémentine. He died in 1908.

Wojciech Weiss gave up music training to study art at the Academy of Fine Arts in Kraków under Leon Wyczółkowski. His family was Polish and in exile in Bukovina. He first painted historical or mythological subjects, then switched to Expressionism after Stanisław Przybyszewski deeply influenced him. He later joined the Vienna Secession, and he was one of the first Polish Art Nouveau poster designers. Near the end of his life he contributed to Socialist realist painting in Poland. His Self-Portrait with Masks dates from 1900.

Alfred Zoff began by studying medicine, though he had decided early to become an artist, and in 1869 he took classes in Graz with the landscape painter Hermann von Königsbrunn. After his father died, his mother moved to Klagenfurt, and he often visited to paint. It remained a favorite place for the rest of his life. He finished his studies in 1890 at Karlsruhe with Gustav Schönleber, who acquainted him with the Barbizon school. From 1907 he was a professor of landscape and still-life painting at the academy in Graz.

After a disagreement about his art studies, George Hayter ran away to sea in 1808 as a midshipman in the Royal Navy. His father, a miniature painter, got him released, and they agreed that George would assist him while pursuing his own studies. In 1809 he secretly married Sarah Milton, a lodger at his father's house. He specialised in portraits and in large works with several hundred individual portraits. Queen Victoria appointed him her Principal Painter in Ordinary and knighted him in 1841.

Until he was twenty, Constant Troyon labored at the minute details of porcelain ornament, because his father was connected with the porcelain manufactory at Sèvres. By twenty-one he was travelling the country painting landscapes for as long as his money lasted. When it ran out, he went back to work as a decorator with the first china manufacturer he met. Only late in life did he find his subject in animals, and then he gained international recognition. He belonged to the Barbizon school and died in 1865.

Henri Lebasque started at the art school in Angers and moved to Paris in 1886, where he studied under Léon Bonnat. He helped Ferdinand Humbert with the murals at the Panthéon and met Camille Pissarro and Auguste Renoir. Contact with Vuillard and Bonnard coloured his vision. From Seurat and Signac he learned a colour theory that used complementary colours in shading. In 1903 he was a founding member of the Salon d'Automne with his friend Henri Matisse. His work hangs in museums in Angers, Lille and Paris.

Hanns Lautensack is sometimes wrongly called Hans Sebald Lautensack. His father Paul was a painter in Bamberg, but the family settled in Nuremberg when he was a child, and he lived there for most of his life. In 1556 he was working in Vienna, perhaps summoned by Emperor Ferdinand I to make pictures of his collection of ancient coins. His etchings carry the monogram H. S. L. They fall into two periods, the Nuremberg years and the Vienna years. His brother Heinrich was a goldsmith.

Adam Perelle learned from his father Gabriel Pérelle and then worked as his assistant. Like his brother Nicolas, he made copperplate engravings of landscapes and monuments. He became engraver of the King and taught drawing and painting in high society, and Louis III, Prince of Condé, was one of his pupils. In 1667 he signed a contract with Erik Dahlbergh. For two Swedish books he made 13 plates of battles and 32 images of landscapes and buildings. He died in 1695.

At twelve Matthijs Maris registered at the Hague Academy of Art but did not pass the entrance exam, so he took lessons from the academy's secretary and was admitted a year later. Queen Sophie's grant helped him follow his brother Jacob to Antwerp, where they rented rooms together. Later the brothers painted in Oosterbeek with Gerard Bilders and Anton Mauve. He began in the Hague School, like his brothers Jacob and Willem, but his later works moved toward a unique style influenced by the Pre-Raphaelites. He died in 1917.

Koloman Moser designed a wide array of things, from postage stamps and magazine vignettes to fashion, stained glass, porcelain, tableware, silver, jewellery and furniture. He was the oldest of three siblings, and he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts and the School of Applied Arts in Vienna, where he also taught from 1899. He drew on the clean lines and repetitive motifs of classical Greek and Roman art, in reaction to the Baroque decadence around him. He was a leading artist of the Vienna Secession and a co-founder of the Wiener Werkstätte. He died in 1918.

Robert Hills studied first under John Alexander Gresse and then enrolled at the Royal Academy of Arts. He mostly painted rural scenes, particularly farm animals. He was also known for drawing animals into the works of other artists, such as George Barret Jr. and George Fennell Robson. His Sketches in Flanders and Holland, with aquatints by himself, was published in 1816. Some of his works are in the British Museum. He lived from 1769 to 1844 and was born in Islington.

Johan Christian Dahl taught Thomas Fearnley, who became a leading representative of Norwegian romantic nationalism in painting. He came from Frederikshald, now Halden, the son of a merchant whose own father had moved from Yorkshire to Norway. His brother Carl Frederik was an astronomer and professor. He married Cecilia Andresen, daughter of his benefactor, the banker Nicolai Andresen. In the autumn of 1841 the couple went to Amsterdam for the birth of their only child. Fearnley died in 1842.

Miklós Barabás painted from an early age and was a pupil of Johann Ender in Vienna for a while. Back in Kolozsvár he learned lithography from Gábor Barra. In Italy he learned watercolour from the Scot William Leighton Leitch, six years older, and the two became friends and toured the Lago Maggiore region together. Leitch influenced his later work. Barabás is mostly known for portraits, among them one of the young Franz Liszt. He settled in Pest in 1855.

Henry Taunt worked first for his father, who was a plumber, but he decided he did not want that trade. From the age of eleven he worked for a tailor, then a stationer, then a bookshop and auction room, all on the High Street in Oxford. At fourteen he joined Edward Bracher, Oxford's first commercial photographer, who for some years had a monopoly in the city. Bracher promoted him from general assistant, and in 1858 Taunt took his first photographs for him. He died in 1922.

According to the RKD, Coenraet Decker was a pupil of Romeyn de Hooghe, and he married Aechje Jans in Sloterdijk when he was 23. He was a Dutch Golden Age engraver from Amsterdam. In the 1670s he worked on the map of Delft, a contract that he won together with Dirk van Bleiswijk for Bleiswijk's Description of Delft. He lived from 1650 to 1685.

Étienne Dupérac arrived in Rome in 1550 and became a skilled designer and engraver there. He is best known for his studies of Rome and its ruins. He published a bird's-eye view of ancient Rome with the buildings reconstructed, one of modern Rome, and a book of forty engravings of Roman monuments, I vestigi dell'antichità di Roma. A book of drawings of Roman ruins set beside reconstructions has been attributed to him, though his authorship has been questioned. He was also an architect, painter and garden designer. He died in 1604.

Jean Audran learned the rudiments of engraving from his father Germain and was then placed with his uncle Gérard Audran in Paris. He showed ability before he was twenty. In 1706 he was made engraver to the king, with a pension and apartments at the Gobelins. His prints include portraits of Louis XV after Gobert, the Duke d'Antin after Rigaud and Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni after Trevisani. He was the brother of Benoit Audran. He was born in Lyons and died in 1756.

Zacharias Dolendo was the brother of Bartholomeus Dolendo, whom he surpassed in style and correctness. He came from Leiden and is said to have been a disciple of Jacob de Gheyn. Some portraits by him are as neat as those by Wierix, and his plates are frequently marked with a cipher. He engraved William, Prince of Orange, in armour, Andromeda chained to the rock after his own design, and a set of small plates of the gods and goddesses copied from larger ones by Goltzius. He lived from 1561 to 1601.

Howard Russell Butler studied science and law before he became a painter. His early training came from William Shannon, and he visited the studio of his uncle William Stanley Haseltine. At Princeton he took a science degree in 1876, stayed on as an assistant professor of physics and rowed on the team. Later he persuaded Andrew Carnegie to fund Carnegie Lake near Princeton, and he painted a solar eclipse for the U.S. Naval Observatory. He also founded the American Fine Arts Society. He died in 1934.

Jean-Pierre Norblin de La Gourdaine started his career in France, but from 1774 to 1796 he lived in Poland, where several of the country's most notable families gave him commissions. His style showed the influence of Watteau and combined the Rococo tradition of fêtes galantes with a panorama of daily life and current political events, captured with journalistic accuracy. He made a gallery of portraits of all social classes in the last years of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Later he became influenced by Rembrandt as well. He died in 1830.

Ludwig Richter was the son of an engraver in Dresden and received his training from him. As a painter he aimed at a thorough blending of the figure with the landscape, as in Ferry at the Schreckenstein. He produced several woodcuts for the Grimm fairy tales, and his work is described as typically German and homely. Erhard and Chodowiecki influenced him strongly, and he stood for both Romanticism and Biedermeier. One of his protégés was Hermann Lungkwitz. He died in 1884.

Willem Claesz. Heda painted only still lifes. He was the son of the Haarlem city architect Claes Pietersz, and his uncle was the painter Cornelis Claesz Heda. Almost nothing is known of his early life, since no surviving pieces are dated to that period, and his earliest known work is a Vanitas. He is known for his innovation of the late breakfast genre of still life, with monochromatic colour and skillful texturing. He died around 1680.

Jan Fyt was the son of a wealthy merchant from Sint-Niklaas who lived in Antwerp. In 1621 he was registered at the Antwerp Guild of St Luke as an apprentice of Hans van den Berghe, who had trained with Goltzius in Haarlem and later with Rubens. He then likely finished his training with the animal painter Frans Snyders. He painted still lifes and animals, and he also combined them, for example game, flowers and fish under a festoon of flowers. He was probably the master of Pieter Boel, who worked in a very similar style.

Dancker Danckerts belonged to a large Amsterdam family of engravers, cartographers, print-sellers and publishers, and his parents were Cornelis Danckerts and Anne Minne of Leiden. He was known for etchings of paintings and maps and for his publications. His works are collected in museums, libraries and archives around the world. He was active in Amsterdam from 1654 to 1666, with a probable trip to Venice in 1656, according to the inscription on a drawing in Parma.

Nils Kreuger's father ran a lumber and wood products business. Illness forced him to leave the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts, and later he studied at Edvard Perséus's private painting school. In 1881 he went to Paris and studied with Jean-Paul Laurens, and he spent much of his time painting outdoors in Grez-sur-Loing. He liked painting at dawn or dusk, in haze or rain. After 1885 he supported the Opponenterna, a group against the outmoded teaching at the Royal Academy, and helped create the Artists' Union. He died in 1930.

Cândido de Faria's father was a physician who specialised in cholera, founded the Hospital de Caridade de Laranjeiras and died in a cholera epidemic. The family moved to Rio de Janeiro, where the boy studied at the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios. He became a caricaturist, painter, lithographer and poster designer, and he emigrated to France in 1882. In France he designed posters for café-chantant performers and the cinema, and also for music scores. After he died in Paris in 1911, his workshop kept going and signed its work Atelier Faria.

Jean Mignon was active from 1537 to the mid-1550s and was one of the first group of artists in France to use etching for prints. He took part in the burst of activity at Fontainebleau in the 1540s. At least half of his prints, over thirty, use compositions by the Italian painter Luca Penni, and others use designs by Primaticcio. In all he made around sixty prints. Nothing is known about his origins or early life. His first appearance in documents is in the royal accounts of 1537, as a painter at the Palace of Fontainebleau.

Kristian Zahrtmann was known especially for history paintings of strong, tragic, legendary women in Danish history. He also painted landscapes, street scenes, folk scenes and portraits. With Peder Severin Krøyer and Theodor Esbern Philipsen he broke away from academicism and from the heritage of the Golden Age of Danish painting, in favor of naturalism and realism. He taught for many years and supported his students' individual styles, which affected the development of Danish art. His bold use of colour dazzled his contemporaries. He was born in Rønne on Bornholm and died in 1917.

Hans Vredeman de Vries is known for his books of ornament and of perspective, the latter from 1604. Born in Leeuwarden, he moved to Mechelen, where he designed ornaments for parades for Charles V and Philip II. He studied Vitruvius and Serlio, in translations by his teacher Pieter Coecke van Aelst, and became an internationally known specialist in perspective. In Antwerp he was appointed city architect and fortification engineer. After 1585 he had to flee the city because of the Spanish occupation, since he was a Protestant. He died in 1607.

Pieter van Bloemen became a master of the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke in 1674, at the age of 17. He was a pupil of Simon Johannes van Douw, by some accounts from the age of 10. Two younger brothers were painters too. He travelled to Rome via Turin with one of them, and in 1688 they were registered in the parish of Sant'Andrea delle Fratte. He painted Italian landscapes with figures, equestrian battles, animals and market scenes. He died in 1720.
